newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: Zairean leaders in South Africa for peace talks.
newsitem.headline: Zairean leaders in South Africa for peace talks.

text.p: Representatives of Zaire's warring parties are about to hold their first face-to-face talks since fighting erupted last year.

South Africa's director general of foreign affairs Rusty Evans told reporters rebel leader Laurent Kabila and a special envoy from Kinshasa arrived in Cape Town late on Wednesday and would meet on Thursday.

The Zairean government said it knew nothing of the talks and has scorned Tuesday's U.N. call for a cease-fire because the Security Council did not condemn neighbouring Rwanda, Uganda and Burundi, which Kinshasa says are aggressors in the conflict.
But Zaire's ailing President Mobutu Sese Seko is believed to have send a nephew, Ngbanda Nzambo Ko Ayumba, to represent him at the talks.
Plans for the meeting were revealed by South African President Nelson Mandela after a regional summit with leaders from Mozambique, Zimbabwe, Botswana and Uganda.

Mandela said Mobutu and Kabila had jointly asked to be allowed to meet in South Africa, but a diplomatic source told Reuters the initiative had come from the Zairean government, which previously had refused to meet the rebels in any forum.

The source said the idea was put to South African Deputy President Thabo Mbeki on Sunday and was followed up on Monday in talks between Mbeki and U.S. Vice President Al Gore, who promoted the proposal.
Evans said U.S. Assistant Secretary of State for Africa George Moose was expected in Cape Town on Thursday to monitor the talks.
He declined to give any details about contacts leading up to the proposed breakthrough talks, saying: "There is a great reluctance on both sides to acknowledge that they are willing to negotiate."
Mandela, who is scheduled to spend Thursday in Johannesburg, said South Africa would offer any assistance sought with Mbeki on hand to assist the two sides.
Evans said Thursday's meeting would be a preliminary exploration of cease-fire proposals made separately by Museveni and the United Nations with little prospect of an immediate breakthrough.

"All parties are agreed that there had to be a step in this direction, but without raising expectations. There is a meeting of minds on the need to bring about a process that could lead to peace in the region," he said.
He said the Cape Town talks would bolster other initiatives including a meeting of African foreign ministers in Kinshasa on Wednesday to follow up on a summit in Nairobi last December.
Ethnic Tutsi rebels took up arms last October accusing the Zairean government of denying them nationality and of seeking to expel them to Rwanda, their ancestral home.
They hold towns and territory along the border with Rwanda, Burundi and Uganda.
Zaire escalated the conflict in January with bombing raids on rebel-held towns and said on Tuesday it had resumed the offensive.
Mandela, elected South Africa's first black president in 1994 and widely regarded as Africa's most influential statesman, initially resisted a role in this and other African crises.

Last year, however, he warned the United States that Africa and not Western powers should drive the peace process on the continent and since then he has actively campaigned for an African peace-making initiative to address all the conflicts in the region, including Angola, Lesotho, Swaziland and the Great Lakes region around Zaire.
Evans said Thursday's talks should be seen as a first step towards Mandela's goal of an African answer to Africa's problems.
